The inner lexicon can be used to expand the model's vocabulary without fine-tuning, reducing token count and maintaining performance.
papers.limitation:
22.6% of multi-token words are never successfully decoded, indicating the inner lexicon does not cover all words.
Vocabulary expansion success rate is lower for morphologically rich languages like Arabic (16%).
papers.abstract: Natural language is composed of words, but modern large language models (LLMs) process sub-words as input. A natural question raised by this discrepancy is whether LLMs encode words internally, and if so how. We present evidence that LLMs engage in an intrinsic detokenization process, where sub-word sequences are combined into coherent whole-word representations at their last token. Our experiments show that this process primarily takes place within the early and middle layers of the model. We further demonstrate its robustness to arbitrary splits (e.g., "cats" to "ca" and "ts"), typos, and importantly-to out-of-vocabulary words: when feeding the last token internal representations of such words to the model as input, it can "understand" them as the complete word despite never seeing such representations as input during training. Our findings suggest that LLMs maintain a latent vocabulary beyond the tokenizer's scope. These insights provide a practical, finetuning-free application for expanding the vocabulary of pre-trained models. By enabling the addition of new vocabulary words, we reduce input length and inference iterations, which reduces both space and model latency, with little to no loss in model accuracy.

papers.title: The wall confronting large language models
papers.research_question: How do scaling laws limit the ability of large language models to improve prediction uncertainty and reliability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the scaling laws of large language models severely limit their ability to improve prediction uncertainty, and proposes a theoretical explanation linking low scaling exponents to non-Gaussian fluctuations, error pileup, and a potential degenerative AI pathway.
papers.conclusion: The degenerative AI pathway is plausible given the scaling laws and theoretical mechanisms, but it can be avoided by prioritizing insight and understanding over brute-force scaling.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling exponents for LLMs are very low (around 0.1), leading to diminishing returns in error reduction with increased compute.
The trade-off between learning (generating non-Gaussian output distributions) and accuracy leads to error pileup and potential information catastrophes.
The Calude-Longo deluge of spurious correlations in large datasets exacerbates the problem by overwhelming true correlations.
The resilience of uncertainty (RoU) in non-Gaussian distributions requires exponentially more data to achieve the same accuracy as Gaussian processes.
Degenerative AI (DAI) is a plausible but avoidable pathway for LLMs if they continue to rely on brute-force scaling without insight.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis is based on simplified models and may not capture all complexities of real LLMs.
future_direction: Prioritize insight and understanding over brute-force scaling.
Use the scientific method to distinguish true correlations from spurious ones in data.
papers.abstract: We show that the scaling laws which determine the performance of large language models (LLMs) severely limit their ability to improve the uncertainty of their predictions. As a result, raising their reliability to meet the standards of scientific inquiry is intractable by any reasonable measure. We argue that the very mechanism which fuels much of the learning power of LLMs, namely the ability to generate non-Gaussian output distributions from Gaussian input ones, might well be at the roots of their propensity to produce error pileup, ensuing information catastrophes and degenerative AI behaviour. This tension between learning and accuracy is a likely candidate mechanism underlying the observed low values of the scaling components. It is substantially compounded by the deluge of spurious correlations pointed out by Calude and Longo which rapidly increase in any data set merely as a function of its size, regardless of its nature. The fact that a degenerative AI pathway is a very probable feature of the LLM landscape does not mean that it must inevitably arise in all future AI research. Its avoidance, which we also discuss in this paper, necessitates putting a much higher premium on insight and understanding of the structural characteristics of the problems being investigated.

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How can lexical semantic knowledge be extracted from pretrained language models, how is this knowledge distributed across layers, and how do the extracted representations compare to traditional static word embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic study of how to extract type-level lexical semantic knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that monolingual models store rich lexical information primarily in lower layers and that extracted vectors can outperform traditional word embeddings on several monolingual tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effectively uncovering this knowledge depends on careful configuration of extraction strategies, with universal best practices including using monolingual LMs, encoding words with multiple contexts, excluding special tokens, and averaging over lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantic knowledge is concentrated in the lower Transformer layers of pretrained language models.
Averaging representations across multiple layers yields better performance than using a single layer.
Monolingual language models contain more lexical information for a target language than massively multilingual models like mBERT.
Extracted 'BERT-based' static word embeddings outperform fastText on monolingual tasks (e.g., lexical similarity, analogy, relation prediction) but not on cross-lingual tasks (BLI, CLIR).
Translation pairs obtain similar representations in independently trained monolingual LMs, indicating approximate isomorphism between the monolingual spaces.
papers.limitation: The comparison with fastText word embeddings is not strictly apples-to-apples because the models were trained on different corpora (Wikipedia dumps for fastText vs. the corpora used for pretraining the LMs).
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect the extraction of word representations and how to sample representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, more lexical semantic probes, and other larger underlying language models.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods, such as layer weighting or attention, and lightweight methods to enrich lexical content in multilingual LMs.
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-ofcontext versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: Does Representation Matter? Exploring Intermediate Layers in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What defines a 'good' representation in large language models, and how does the quality of intermediate representations compare to final layers across different architectures and settings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that intermediate layers of LLMs often provide better representations for downstream tasks than final layers, and reveals significant differences in representation quality and evolution between Transformer and State Space Model (SSM) architectures.
papers.conclusion: The research advances understanding of internal representation dynamics in LLMs, highlighting the pivotal role of intermediate layers and the distinct behaviors of Transformer and SSM architectures, providing guidance for model optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently outperform final layers on downstream embedding tasks from the MTEB benchmark.
Prompt entropy in intermediate layers is negatively correlated with MMLU performance for Transformers like Llama3, but not for SSMs like Mamba2.
Transformers exhibit greater representational variability and information compression in intermediate layers, while SSMs show more stable representations across layers.
Training effects on representation quality are most pronounced in intermediate layers, with prompt entropy decreasing and InfoNCE peaking as training progresses.
Extreme input conditions (token repetition, randomness, and length) distinctly affect prompt entropy, particularly in intermediate layers, and a bimodal entropy distribution is observed in Transformer intermediate layers with an unknown cause.
papers.limitation: The cause of the bimodal entropy distribution observed in intermediate layers of Transformer models remains unknown.
future_direction: Investigate the causes of bimodal entropy distributions in intermediate layers.
Explore the development of new metrics specifically tailored to LLMs for representation evaluation.
papers.abstract: Understanding what defines a good representation in large language models (LLMs) is fundamental to both theoretical understanding and practical applications. In this paper, we investigate the quality of intermediate representations in various LLM architectures, including Transformers and State Space Models (SSMs). We find that intermediate layers often yield more informative representations for downstream tasks than the final layers. To measure the representation quality, we adapt and apply a suite of metrics - such as prompt entropy, curvature, and augmentation-invariance - originally proposed in other contexts. Our empirical study reveals significant architectural differences, how representations evolve throughout training, and how factors like input randomness and prompt length affect each layer. Notably, we observe a bimodal pattern in the entropy of some intermediate layers and consider potential explanations tied to training data. Overall, our results illuminate the internal mechanics of LLMs and guide strategies for architectural optimization and training.

papers.title: The Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference?
papers.research_question: What is the robustness of Large Language Models (LLMs) to structural interventions like layer deletion and swapping, and can this inform a framework for depth-dependent computations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes a four-stage framework (detokenization, feature engineering, prediction ensembling, residual sharpening) for interpreting depth-dependent computations in LLMs, based on behavioral and mechanistic evidence from layer-wise interventions.
papers.conclusion: This work introduces a four-stage framework for understanding inference in LLMs, which emerges across architectures and scales, suggesting transformers perform inference as an ordered composition of specialized computational regimes.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are remarkably robust to layer deletion and swapping, retaining 72–95% of original top-1 accuracy without fine-tuning.
Performance degradation is not uniform: early and final layers are most sensitive, while middle layers are robust to interventions.
The pattern of sensitivity and other analyses motivate a hypothesis of four universal stages of inference observed across model families and sizes.
Evidence for each stage includes: early layers exhibit local attention and subjoiner heads (detokenization); middle layers show peak probing accuracy for semantic features (feature engineering); later layers show prediction and suppression neurons (ensembling and sharpening).
The residual architecture enables redundancy and self-repair, explaining the model's robustness to local interventions.
papers.limitation: Stage boundaries are approximate, and multiple stages may co-occur within a single layer. The framework reflects aggregate trends, whereas individual tokens may follow distinct processing paths.
future_direction: Future work can sharpen the stage boundaries.
Future work can link the stages to optimization dynamics.
Future work can provide a more theoretical framework.
papers.abstract: We investigate the robustness of Large Language Models (LLMs) to structural interventions by deleting and swapping adjacent layers during inference. Surprisingly, models retain 72-95% of their original top-1 prediction accuracy without any fine-tuning. We find that performance degradation is not uniform across layers: interventions to the early and final layers cause the most degradation, while the model is remarkably robust to dropping middle layers. This pattern of localized sensitivity motivates our hypothesis of four stages of inference, observed across diverse model families and sizes: (1) detokenization, where local context is integrated to lift raw token embeddings into higher-level representations; (2) feature engineering, where task- and entity-specific features are iteratively refined; (3) prediction ensembling, where hidden states are aggregated into plausible next-token predictions; and (4) residual sharpening, where irrelevant features are suppressed to finalize the output distribution. Synthesizing behavioral and mechanistic evidence, we provide a framework for interpreting depth-dependent computations in LLMs.

papers.title: On Efficient Transformer-Based Image Pre-training for Low-Level Vision
papers.research_question: How does pre-training act in image processing systems (low-level vision tasks) and what are effective pre-training strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes how pre-training affects internal representations in low-level vision tasks and finds that multi-related-task pre-training is more effective and data-efficient than other strategies.
papers.conclusion: Pre-training plays a central role in developing stronger intermediate representations by incorporating more local information, and its effect is task-specific. Multi-related-task pre-training is highly effective and data-efficient for low-level vision.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-training introduces more local information to higher layers in super-resolution and deraining, yielding significant performance gains, while it hardly affects internal feature representations in denoising, resulting in limited gains.
Multi-related-task pre-training is more effective and data-efficient than single-task or multi-unrelated-task pre-training.
Larger model capacities generally obtain more improvements from pre-training.
Transformers benefit more from pre-training than CNNs, providing higher performance baselines with fewer parameters.
The internal representations of SR and deraining models show clear stages (more local in early layers, more global in higher layers), while denoising models present a relatively uniform structure filled with local information.
papers.limitation:
The study mainly investigates pre-training on synthesized data; future research should explore real-world settings and more tasks, extended to video processing.
The encoder-decoder design uses a fixed downsampling strategy, which may not be optimal for all degradation levels; adaptive downsampling could be better.
future_direction: Explore pre-training in real-world settings and more tasks.
Extend the study to video processing.
Investigate adaptive downsampling based on degradation degrees.
papers.abstract: Pre-training has marked numerous state of the arts in high-level computer vision, while few attempts have ever been made to investigate how pre-training acts in image processing systems. In this paper, we tailor transformer-based pre-training regimes that boost various low-level tasks. To comprehensively diagnose the influence of pre-training, we design a whole set of principled evaluation tools that uncover its effects on internal representations. The observations demonstrate that pre-training plays strikingly different roles in low-level tasks. For example, pre-training introduces more local information to higher layers in super-resolution (SR), yielding significant performance gains, while pre-training hardly affects internal feature representations in denoising, resulting in limited gains. Further, we explore different methods of pre-training, revealing that multi-related-task pre-training is more effective and data-efficient than other alternatives. Finally, we extend our study to varying data scales and model sizes, as well as comparisons between transformers and CNNs-based architectures. Based on the study, we successfully develop state-of-the-art models for multiple low-level tasks. Code is released at https://github.com/fenglinglwb/EDT.

papers.title: Algorithmic Capabilities of Random Transformers
papers.research_question: To what extent do the circuits that implement interpretable procedures in transformers depend on the supervisory signal provided during training, and to what extent are they attributable to behavior already present in models at initialization?
papers.core_contribution: Randomly initialized transformers, with only their embedding and unembedding layers trained, can successfully perform a range of algorithmic and language modeling tasks, indicating that these capabilities are inherent to the transformer architecture and accessible at initialization via appropriate input encodings.
papers.conclusion: Transformer models possess inherent algorithmic capabilities at initialization that can be accessed by training only their embedding layers, suggesting that some interpretable circuits are present even before training and highlighting the strong inductive bias of the architecture.
papers.key_findings:
Random transformers with embedding-only training achieve perfect accuracy on modular addition, needle-in-a-haystack, decimal addition, and parenthesis balancing tasks.
They outperform fully trained LSTMs on some algorithmic tasks and exhibit interpretable attention patterns similar to induction heads.
Learned embeddings for tasks like modular addition form structured low-dimensional representations (e.g., circles).
Random transformers can memorize arbitrary associations but with lower parameter efficiency than fully trained transformers.
They can generate grammatical natural language text, though with lower coherence and perplexity than fully trained models.
papers.limitation:
The space of architectural decisions (model size, attention mechanisms, normalization, tokenization) is large, and the described trends may change with different parameterizations.
The analysis focuses on standard transformers and does not address whether trends hold in other architectures like linear attention or state-space models.
The subspace analysis uses linear PCA and may not capture non-linear subspaces or latent semantics.
future_direction: Investigate how learned feature codebooks and automated neuron labeling procedures behave when applied to random transformers.
Closer study of untrained models as a source of insight for improving neural model architectures.
papers.abstract: Trained transformer models have been found to implement interpretable procedures for tasks like arithmetic and associative recall, but little is understood about how the circuits that implement these procedures originate during training. To what extent do they depend on the supervisory signal provided to models, and to what extent are they attributable to behavior already present in models at the beginning of training? To investigate these questions, we investigate what functions can be learned by randomly initialized transformers in which only the embedding layers are optimized, so that the only input--output mappings learnable from data are those already implemented (up to a choice of encoding scheme) by the randomly initialized model. We find that these random transformers can perform a wide range of meaningful algorithmic tasks, including modular arithmetic, in-weights and in-context associative recall, decimal addition, parenthesis balancing, and even some aspects of natural language text generation. Our results indicate that some algorithmic capabilities are present in transformers (and accessible via appropriately structured inputs) even before these models are trained. Code is available at https://github.com/fjzzq2002/random_transformers.

papers.title: Finding the input features that reduce the entropy of a neural network’s prediction
papers.research_question: How can we identify input features that have the most impact on the entropy (uncertainty) of a neural network's prediction in image classification?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an explainability method (OMIG) that identifies input features which reduce the prediction entropy of a neural network classifier, and proposes a metric for the quantitative comparison of explainability methods based on their impact on entropy.
papers.conclusion: The introduced OMIG method effectively highlights input features that reduce the entropy of neural network predictions, producing interpretable heatmaps and demonstrating superior quantitative performance in entropy reduction compared to established explainability techniques.
papers.key_findings:
OMIG produces heatmaps that highlight features leading to a more consistent reduction in prediction entropy compared to other explainability methods like Guided Backpropagation, Integrated Gradients, Sensitivity Analysis, and Gradient SHAP.
OMIG achieves the best performance under the Selectivity criterion for the ImageNet-V2 dataset.
The visual quality of OMIG heatmaps is comparable to or better than other methods, often highlighting larger parts of the relevant object compared to edge-focused methods like Guided Backpropagation.
The performance of Integrated Gradients is highly dependent on the image background, performing well only when the background is near zero.
The proposed quantitative metric (Equation 6) shows that features highlighted by OMIG lead to a more consistent entropy reduction across different datasets and perturbation scales.
papers.limitation:
The OMIG method relies on hyperparameters (ε, c, n_samples) that require fine-tuning for each dataset, which influences the visual quality of the heatmaps.
The entropy measure used only captures aleatoric uncertainty, not epistemic uncertainty.
OMIG is computationally more expensive than single backward-pass methods like Guided Backpropagation or Saliency, though still practical (a few seconds per image).
future_direction: Determining best practices or natural choices for the OMIG hyperparameters that work across different datasets.
Extending the OMIG method to highlight features that affect other quantities, such as the epistemic uncertainty of Bayesian neural networks.
papers.abstract: Abstract In deep learning-based image classification, the entropy of a neural network’s output is often taken as a measure of its uncertainty. We introduce an explainability method that identifies those features in the input that impact most this uncertainty. Learning the corresponding features by straightforward backpropagation typically leads to results that are hard to interpret. We propose an extension of the recently proposed oriented, modified integrated gradients (OMIG) technique as an alternative to produce perturbations of the input that have a visual quality comparable to explainability methods from the literature but marks features that have a substantially higher impact on the entropy. The potential benefits of the modified OMIG method are demonstrated by comparison with current state-of-the-art explainability methods on several popular databases. In addition to a qualitative analysis of explainability results, we propose a metric for their quantitative comparison, which evaluates the impact of identified features on the entropy of a prediction.

papers.title: Neural Population Geometry Reveals the Role of Stochasticity in Robust Perception
papers.research_question: How do adversarial perturbations influence the internal representations of standard, adversarially trained, and biologically-inspired stochastic networks, and what are the geometric signatures of robustness in these networks?
papers.core_contribution: Using manifold analysis, the paper reveals distinct geometric signatures of robustness in standard, adversarially trained, and stochastic networks, and shows that stochasticity leads to overlap between clean and adversarial representations, mediating a tradeoff between clean and adversarial performance.
papers.conclusion: Neural population geometry reveals different mechanisms of robustness in adversarially trained and stochastic networks, and stochasticity can be beneficial for robust perception in both machine and biological computation.
papers.key_findings:
Standard, adversarially trained, and stochastic networks each have distinct geometric signatures in response to clean and adversarially perturbed stimuli.
Stochasticity in auditory networks also improves robustness and shows similar geometric trends as in vision.
Stochastic networks exhibit overlap between representations of clean and adversarial stimuli, which contributes to robustness.
There is a tradeoff between clean and adversarial performance mediated by competing geometric effects of stochasticity.
papers.abstract: Adversarial examples are often cited by neuroscientists and machine learning researchers as an example of how computational models diverge from biological sensory systems. Recent work has proposed adding biologically-inspired components to visual neural networks as a way to improve their adversarial robustness. One surprisingly effective component for reducing adversarial vulnerability is response stochasticity, like that exhibited by biological neurons. Here, using recently developed geometrical techniques from computational neuroscience, we investigate how adversarial perturbations influence the internal representations of standard, adversarially trained, and biologically-inspired stochastic networks. We find distinct geometric signatures for each type of network, revealing different mechanisms for achieving robust representations. Next, we generalize these results to the auditory domain, showing that neural stochasticity also makes auditory models more robust to adversarial perturbations. Geometric analysis of the stochastic networks reveals overlap between representations of clean and adversarially perturbed stimuli, and quantitatively demonstrates that competing geometric effects of stochasticity mediate a tradeoff between adversarial and clean performance. Our results shed light on the strategies of robust perception utilized by adversarially trained and stochastic networks, and help explain how stochasticity may be beneficial to machine and biological computation.

papers.title: From Loops to Oops: Fallback Behaviors of Language Models Under Uncertainty
papers.research_question: What is the connection between undesirable LLM behaviors (hallucinations, degenerate text, repetitions) as fallbacks under epistemic uncertainty, and how do they shift with model strength and during generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fallback behaviors (sequence repetitions, degenerate text, hallucinations) follow a consistent ordering and shift from simpler to more complex forms as model strength increases (via more parameters, pretraining tokens, or instruction tuning), and during a single generation as uncertainty rises.
papers.conclusion: Fallback behaviors are inherent to LLMs under epistemic uncertainty, and current decoding methods that reduce degenerate text often increase subtler and potentially more harmful hallucinations, making model uncertainty harder to detect.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models (more parameters) shift fallback behavior from sequence repetitions to hallucinations.
Models that train longer (see more pretraining tokens) shift from repetitions to hallucinations.
Instruction finetuning shifts fallback behaviors from repetitions to hallucinations.
During a single generation, models shift from correct answers to hallucinations and then to repetitions as uncertainty increases.
Random sampling (e.g., temperature sampling) reduces repetitions but increases hallucinations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit undesirable behaviors, such as hallucinations and sequence repetitions. We propose to view these behaviors as fallbacks that models exhibit under epistemic uncertainty, and investigate the connection between them. We categorize fallback behaviors - sequence repetitions, degenerate text, and hallucinations - and extensively analyze them in models from the same family that differ by the amount of pretraining tokens, parameter count, or the inclusion of instruction-following training. Our experiments reveal a clear and consistent ordering of fallback behaviors, across all these axes: the more advanced an LLM is (i.e., trained on more tokens, has more parameters, or instruction-tuned), its fallback behavior shifts from sequence repetitions, to degenerate text, and then to hallucinations. Moreover, the same ordering is observed during the generation of a single sequence, even for the best-performing models; as uncertainty increases, models shift from generating hallucinations to producing degenerate text and finally sequence repetitions. Lastly, we demonstrate that while common decoding techniques, such as random sampling, alleviate unwanted behaviors like sequence repetitions, they increase harder-to-detect hallucinations.

papers.title: TokenSHAP: Interpreting Large Language Models with Monte Carlo Shapley Value Estimation
papers.research_question: How can large language models be interpreted by attributing importance to individual tokens or substrings within input prompts using Shapley values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TokenSHAP, a method for interpreting LLMs by estimating Shapley values for token importance using Monte Carlo sampling, providing a quantitative, model-agnostic framework for token attribution.
papers.conclusion: TokenSHAP advances LLM interpretability by adapting Shapley values to natural language processing with Monte Carlo estimation, offering a scalable solution for understanding token importance and enhancing model transparency and accountability.
papers.key_findings:
TokenSHAP effectively distinguishes between relevant and irrelevant tokens in prompts with injected random words, outperforming baseline methods like random attribution and prompt engineering.
Monte Carlo sampling with first-order omission conditions improves the accuracy and stability of Shapley value approximations, balancing computational efficiency and fidelity.
TokenSHAP provides interpretable, quantitative measures of token importance that align with human judgments and are faithful to model behavior.
The method is model-agnostic and can be applied without access to internal model architecture, enhancing transparency for black-box models.
TokenSHAP enables visualization of token importance through color-coded representations, aiding in intuitive understanding of model decisions.
papers.limitation:
Computational cost due to repeated model evaluations
Sensitivity to sampling introduces variability in importance scores
Assumption of additivity may not hold for complex token interactions
future_direction: Exploring alternative value functions for better semantic similarity capture
Investigating Shapley value stability across different LLM architectures and input sizes
Developing interactive tools for dynamic exploration of token importance
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly prevalent in critical applications, the need for interpretable AI has grown. We introduce TokenSHAP, a novel method for interpreting LLMs by attributing importance to individual tokens or substrings within input prompts. This approach adapts Shapley values from cooperative game theory to natural language processing, offering a rigorous framework for understanding how different parts of an input contribute to a model's response. TokenSHAP leverages Monte Carlo sampling for computational efficiency, providing interpretable, quantitative measures of token importance. We demonstrate its efficacy across diverse prompts and LLM architectures, showing consistent improvements over existing baselines in alignment with human judgments, faithfulness to model behavior, and consistency. Our method's ability to capture nuanced interactions between tokens provides valuable insights into LLM behavior, enhancing model transparency, improving prompt engineering, and aiding in the development of more reliable AI systems. TokenSHAP represents a significant step towards the necessary interpretability for responsible AI deployment, contributing to the broader goal of creating more transparent, accountable, and trustworthy AI systems.

papers.title: Analysis of Self-Attention Head Diversity for Conformer-based Automatic Speech Recognition
papers.research_question: What is the diversity of attention heads in Conformer-based ASR models, and how can it be increased to improve performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that attention heads in Conformer-based ASR models become highly correlated during training, and that adding diversity-promoting auxiliary loss functions during training increases head diversity and improves word error rate.
papers.conclusion: Attention heads in Conformer-based ASR models become correlated during training, and promoting diversity through auxiliary losses reduces redundancy and improves performance.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in Conformer-based ASR models become highly correlated during training, with attention probabilities showing the highest correlation.
Mixing different attention mechanisms does not automatically ensure diversity or improve WER.
Introducing diversity-promoting auxiliary loss functions during training reduces head correlation and improves WER by up to 6% relative.
More diverse attention heads receive more diverse gradients during backpropagation.
papers.abstract: Attention layers are an integral part of modern end-to-end automatic speech recognition systems, for instance as part of the Transformer or Conformer architecture. Attention is typically multi-headed, where each head has an independent set of learned parameters and operates on the same input feature sequence. The output of multi-headed attention is a fusion of the outputs from the individual heads. We empirically analyze the diversity between representations produced by the different attention heads and demonstrate that the heads become highly correlated during the course of training. We investigate a few approaches to increasing attention head diversity, including using different attention mechanisms for each head and auxiliary training loss functions to promote head diversity. We show that introducing diversity-promoting auxiliary loss functions during training is a more effective approach, and obtain WER improvements of up to 6% relative on the Librispeech corpus. Finally, we draw a connection between the diversity of attention heads and the similarity of the gradients of head parameters.

papers.title: Visualizing the Diversity of Representations Learned by Bayesian Neural Networks
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether global XAI methods can visualize the diversity of BNN instances, how the choice of Bayesian inference method affects feature visualization diversity, whether feature visualization diversity correlates with uncertainty estimates, and how network width affects the diversity in multimodal posteriors.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that global XAI methods can visualize the diversity of decision-making strategies in Bayesian Neural Networks, and that this diversity correlates with uncertainty estimates and is affected by the choice of Bayesian inference method and network width.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that global XAI methods can effectively visualize and quantify the diversity of representations in BNNs, providing human-understandable insights into posterior distributions and confirming theoretical predictions.
papers.key_findings:
Global XAI methods can be applied to explain the diversity of decision-making strategies of BNN instances.
Monte Carlo dropout with commonly used dropout rates exhibits increased diversity in feature representations compared to the multimodal posterior approximation of MultiSWAG.
The diversity of learned feature representations highly correlates with the uncertainty estimate for the output.
The inter-mode diversity of the multimodal posterior decreases as the network width increases, while the intra-mode diversity increases.
papers.limitation: Feature visualizations depend on hyperparameters and initialization of the Activation Maximization optimization.
papers.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) aims to make learning machines less opaque, and offers researchers and practitioners various tools to reveal the decision-making strategies of neural networks. In this work, we investigate how XAI methods can be used for exploring and visualizing the diversity of feature representations learned by Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). Our goal is to provide a global understanding of BNNs by making their decision-making strategies a) visible and tangible through feature visualizations and b) quantitatively measurable with a distance measure learned by contrastive learning. Our work provides new insights into the \emph{posterior} distribution in terms of human-understandable feature information with regard to the underlying decision making strategies. The main findings of our work are the following: 1) global XAI methods can be applied to explain the diversity of decision-making strategies of BNN instances, 2) Monte Carlo dropout with commonly used Dropout rates exhibit increased diversity in feature representations compared to the multimodal posterior approximation of MultiSWAG, 3) the diversity of learned feature representations highly correlates with the uncertainty estimate for the output and 4) the inter-mode diversity of the multimodal posterior decreases as the network width increases, while the intra mode diversity increases. These findings are consistent with the recent Deep Neural Networks theory, providing additional intuitions about what the theory implies in terms of humanly understandable concepts.

papers.title: Quiet Feature Learning in Algorithmic Tasks
papers.research_question: Do Transformer-based models learn meaningful internal representations (quiet features) before showing improvement in task loss, and are these features causally necessary for performance?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer-based models learn 'quiet features' (intermediate algorithmic computations) during a slow phase where task loss is stagnant, and these features are causally necessary for the subsequent sharp drop in loss.
papers.conclusion: Transformer-based models encode important intermediate computations well before they show significant gains in next-token prediction, revealing a gap between internal representation learning and external task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Phase transitions occur during learning: validation loss shows a slow phase with minimal improvement followed by a fast phase of rapid decrease.
Quiet features, representing intermediate algorithmic computations, are learned during the slow phase before any decrease in task loss.
Ablation experiments show that quiet features are causally necessary for task performance.
Feature learning curves can exhibit a U-shape, where probing loss for some quiet features increases after the phase transition, suggesting representation changes.
Phase transitions are observed across different compute budgets, model sizes, dataset sizes, and within individual training runs.
future_direction: Developing theoretical frameworks to explain why models accumulate latent subroutines before observable metric improvements.
Extending the analysis to larger, more complex models and natural-language settings.
Motivating new methods for probing and monitoring internal learning dynamics.
papers.abstract: We train Transformer-based language models on ten foundational algorithmic tasks and observe pronounced phase transitions in their loss curves that deviate from established power-law scaling trends. Over large ranges of compute, the validation loss barely improves, then abruptly decreases. Probing the models' internal representations reveals that quiet features are learned prior to any decrease in task loss. These quiet features represent intermediate algorithmic computations that do not by themselves improve the output loss. Ablation experiments demonstrate that individual quiet features are causally necessary for task performance. Our results demonstrate that substantial representational progress can remain hidden beneath an apparently flat loss curve, challenging the prevailing use of cross-entropy as a proxy for learning and motivating richer diagnostics for monitoring model training.

papers.title: Generation Space Size: Understanding and Calibrating Open-Endedness of LLM Generations
papers.research_question: How can we measure and calibrate the generation space size of LLMs to address failure modes like output homogeneity and hallucination?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GSSBench, an evaluation framework for measuring generation space size, and shows that EigenScore is a good proxy for GSS, with applications in grounding, reasoning analysis, and diversity optimization.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces GSS as a unifying framework for model failures and presents GSSBench for evaluation, showing that EigenScore is a strong proxy for GSS and has applications in multiple domains.
papers.key_findings:
EigenScore variants (E_output and E_average) are the best-performing metrics for approximating a model's generation space size (GSS).
Larger models are not necessarily better calibrated in terms of GSS; for example, Qwen3-0.6B outperforms Qwen3-8B on GSSBench.
GSS, as measured by EigenScore, can separate ambiguous from non-ambiguous prompts and predict when a model will ask clarification questions.
GSS is positively correlated with reasoning token length in deductive reasoning tasks, providing insight into model representations.
Leave-One-Out EigenScore can be used in a reward function to steer models towards generating more diverse outputs while maintaining quality.
papers.abstract: Different open-ended generation tasks require different degrees of output diversity. However, current LLMs are often miscalibrated. They collapse to overly homogeneous outputs for creative tasks and hallucinate diverse but incorrect responses for factual tasks. We argue that these two failure modes are unified by, and can both be addressed by, the notion of effective generation space size (GSS) -- the set of semantically distinct outputs a model considers for a prompt. We present GSSBench, a task suite of prompt pairs with ground-truth GSS relationships to assess different metrics and understand where models diverge from desired behavior. We find that hallucination detection metrics, particularly EigenScore, consistently outperform standard diversity and uncertainty quantification metrics, while using only model internals, providing interpretable insights into a model's internal task representations. We demonstrate three applications of GSS: (1) detecting prompt ambiguity and predicting clarification questions for better grounding, (2) interpreting overthinking and underthinking in reasoning models, and (3) steering models to expand their generation space to yield high-quality and diverse outputs.

papers.title: Peripheral Vision Transformer
papers.research_question: How can we model human peripheral vision in deep neural networks for visual recognition by incorporating peripheral inductive biases into self-attention layers?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Peripheral Vision Transformer (PerViT), which incorporates peripheral inductive biases into vision transformers via a new Multi-head Peripheral Attention (MPA) mechanism, enabling the network to learn to partition the visual field into diverse peripheral regions for improved image classification performance and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that incorporating peripheral inductive biases into vision transformers via the proposed Multi-head Peripheral Attention leads to effective visual recognition, with the model learning to perceive visual elements in a manner similar to human peripheral vision.
papers.key_findings:
The network learns to attend to different peripheral regions (central, para-central, mid, far) in different layers and heads, mimicking human peripheral vision without special supervision.
Early layers focus on central regions (local attention) while later layers focus on peripheral regions (global attention), with this tendency becoming more pronounced in larger models.
The position-based attention (Φp) plays two roles: it acts as a semi-dynamic attention mechanism in early layers and as a position bias injection in later layers.
PerViT outperforms baseline columnar transformers (e.g., DeiT) in image classification across different model sizes, demonstrating the efficacy of the proposed peripheral attention mechanism.
The proposed peripheral initialization facilitates training by imposing strong locality in early layers and global attention in later layers at the start of training.
papers.limitation:
Training vision transformers from scratch on large-scale datasets demands substantial computational resources, leading to environmental concerns related to CO2 emissions.
The work focuses solely on image classification, leaving other high-level vision tasks (e.g., object detection, segmentation, action recognition) for future work.
future_direction: Applying the proposed biologically-inspired approach to other high-level vision tasks such as object detection, segmentation, and action recognition.
papers.abstract: Human vision possesses a special type of visual processing systems called peripheral vision. Partitioning the entire visual field into multiple contour regions based on the distance to the center of our gaze, the peripheral vision provides us the ability to perceive various visual features at different regions. In this work, we take a biologically inspired approach and explore to model peripheral vision in deep neural networks for visual recognition. We propose to incorporate peripheral position encoding to the multi-head self-attention layers to let the network learn to partition the visual field into diverse peripheral regions given training data. We evaluate the proposed network, dubbed PerViT, on ImageNet-1K and systematically investigate the inner workings of the model for machine perception, showing that the network learns to perceive visual data similarly to the way that human vision does. The performance improvements in image classification over the baselines across different model sizes demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method.

papers.title: Towards Uncovering How Large Language Model Works: An Explainability Perspective
papers.research_question: How can explainability techniques uncover the internal mechanisms of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This survey paper provides a systematic overview of existing explainability techniques, including mechanistic interpretability and representation engineering, to uncover the inner workings of large language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that explainability techniques like mechanistic interpretability and representation engineering are crucial for understanding LLMs, but there are still challenges such as scalability and evaluation of explanations.
papers.limitation: The survey does not explore the complete landscape of relevant XAI methods for understanding LLMs, due to space constraints.
future_direction: Developing scalable techniques to analyze and interpret the intricate knowledge structures embedded within LLMs.
Revealing the intricate mechanisms that give rise to advanced reasoning capabilities in LLMs.
Fully leveraging insights from explainability to develop techniques that can substantially improve LLM performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have led to breakthroughs in language tasks, yet the internal mechanisms that enable their remarkable generalization and reasoning abilities remain opaque. This lack of transparency presents challenges such as hallucinations, toxicity, and misalignment with human values, hindering the safe and beneficial deployment of LLMs. This paper aims to uncover the mechanisms underlying LLM functionality through the lens of explainability. First, we review how knowledge is architecturally composed within LLMs and encoded in their internal parameters via mechanistic interpretability techniques. Then, we summarize how knowledge is embedded in LLM representations by leveraging probing techniques and representation engineering. Additionally, we investigate the training dynamics through a mechanistic perspective to explain phenomena such as grokking and memorization. Lastly, we explore how the insights gained from these explanations can enhance LLM performance through model editing, improve efficiency through pruning, and better align with human values.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Measures of Information Reflect Memorization Patterns
papers.research_question: Does the diversity in neural activation patterns, quantified by information-theoretic measures (entropy and mutual information), reflect model generalization and memorization (heuristic and example-level)?
papers.core_contribution: Information organization in neural activations, measured by entropy and mutual information, distinguishes between heuristic memorization (low entropy, high MI) and example-level memorization (high entropy, low MI), and can be used for model selection without labeled data.
papers.conclusion: Information-theoretic measures of neural activations can distinguish between models that show heuristic memorization and example-level memorization, and offer a potential intrinsic evaluation strategy for model selection.
papers.key_findings:
Networks exhibiting heuristic memorization (learning spurious correlations) show low intra-neuron and inter-neuron diversity, reflected in low entropy and high mutual information (MI).
Networks exhibiting example-level memorization (overfitting to individual examples) show high intra-neuron and inter-neuron diversity, reflected in high entropy and low MI.
These patterns hold across natural language and vision tasks, and for activations computed on unlabeled in-distribution examples.
The information measures correlate with model generalization rankings from domain-specific evaluation metrics, demonstrating utility for model selection.
The findings are comparative and require a reference model or known memorization type for practical application.
papers.limitation:
The findings are comparative and require a-priori knowledge of a well-generalizing model or the expected type of memorization to benchmark against.
The measures might not be directly comparable across models of different families, architectures, or capacities.
More research is needed to study the scaling behavior of these measures to larger models.
future_direction: Investigate the scaling behavior of information measures as a function of data and model size.
Explore applications in out-of-distribution (OOD) detection using point-wise versions of the measures.
Investigate regularizing models by constraining MI/entropy values to a certain band to improve generalization.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are known to exploit spurious artifacts (or shortcuts) that co-occur with a target label, exhibiting heuristic memorization. On the other hand, networks have been shown to memorize training examples, resulting in example-level memorization. These kinds of memorization impede generalization of networks beyond their training distributions. Detecting such memorization could be challenging, often requiring researchers to curate tailored test sets. In this work, we hypothesize -- and subsequently show -- that the diversity in the activation patterns of different neurons is reflective of model generalization and memorization. We quantify the diversity in the neural activations through information-theoretic measures and find support for our hypothesis on experiments spanning several natural language and vision tasks. Importantly, we discover that information organization points to the two forms of memorization, even for neural activations computed on unlabelled in-distribution examples. Lastly, we demonstrate the utility of our findings for the problem of model selection. The associated code and other resources for this work are available at https://rachitbansal.github.io/information-measures.

papers.title: Dynamical Systems Analysis Reveals Functional Regimes in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can neuroscience-inspired dynamical metrics (hierarchical integration and metastability) reliably characterise differences in computational organisation across functional regimes in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a composite dynamical index (Ψ′), combining hierarchical integration and metastability adapted from neuroscience, can distinguish functional regimes (structured reasoning, repetition, noisy sampling, architectural perturbations) in LLM internal activations.
papers.conclusion: Neuroscience-inspired dynamical metrics can distinguish functional regimes in LLMs, with structured reasoning exhibiting higher temporal integration and metastability, indicating these formal properties capture aspects of computational organisation.
papers.key_findings:
Structured reasoning prompts consistently yield a higher composite dynamical index (Ψ′) compared to repetitive, noisy, and perturbed generation regimes.
The composite index is robust to layer selection, random channel subsampling, and random seeds, indicating it captures distributed system-level properties.
Component-level analysis reveals a dissociation: architectural perturbations preserve long-range temporal correlations (integration) but reduce coordination flexibility (metastability).
The metric most reliably distinguishes structured reasoning from destabilised noisy sampling, with a large effect size (d=1.82).
The dynamical properties of integration and metastability, central to neuroscience, are measurable and informative in artificial neural systems like transformers.
papers.limitation:
Temporal resolution is constrained by autoregressive generation (256 tokens), limiting reliable estimation of cross-frequency coupling.
Frequency bands for metastability were selected empirically, lacking a principled mapping between oscillatory scales and transformer dynamics.
Channel selection was random; targeted selection strategies may improve sensitivity.
The equal weighting of integration and metastability in the composite index was theoretically motivated but not optimised.
The functional relevance of Ψ′ for task performance remains to be established.
Experimental conditions bundle factors (lexical diversity, output entropy, periodicity) that may influence Ψ′, limiting causal attribution to 'reasoning' per se.
future_direction: Extending the analysis across model scales, architectures, and training regimes to test generality.
Methodological extensions using longer sequences or alternative estimators to incorporate cross-frequency coupling and compare with established neuroscience frameworks.
Validating Ψ′ against behavioural performance, trial-level output quality, targeted ablations, and alternative dynamical measures (e.g., entropy rates, Lyapunov exponents, dimensionality metrics).
Applying the approach to other sequence domains (e.g., audio, video, multimodal models).
papers.abstract: Large language models perform text generation through high-dimensional internal dynamics, yet the temporal organisation of these dynamics remains poorly understood. Most interpretability approaches emphasise static representations or causal interventions, leaving temporal structure largely unexplored. Drawing on neuroscience, where temporal integration and metastability are core markers of neural organisation, we adapt these concepts to transformer models and discuss a composite dynamical metric, computed from activation time-series during autoregressive generation. We evaluate this metric in GPT-2-medium across five conditions: structured reasoning, forced repetition, high-temperature noisy sampling, attention-head pruning, and weight-noise injection. Structured reasoning consistently exhibits elevated metric relative to repetitive, noisy, and perturbed regimes, with statistically significant differences confirmed by one-way ANOVA and large effect sizes in key comparisons. These results are robust to layer selection, channel subsampling, and random seeds. Our findings demonstrate that neuroscience-inspired dynamical metrics can reliably characterise differences in computational organisation across functional regimes in large language models. We stress that the proposed metric captures formal dynamical properties and does not imply subjective experience.

papers.title: Representation in large language models
papers.research_question: Is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, contrary to the look-up table view, and outlines how mechanistic interpretability methods can be used to study these representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do use representation-based information processing, and we can investigate these representations using mechanistic interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
The look-up table view of LLMs is inadequate because it cannot explain robust behavior.
Representations, as defined by four conditions (INFORMATION, EXPLOITABILITY, BEHAVIOR, ROLE), can explain robust behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability methods like probing and causal interventions can test for representations in LLMs.
papers.abstract: The extraordinary success of recent Large Language Models (LLMs) on a diverse array of tasks has led to an explosion of scientific and philosophical theorizing aimed at explaining how they do what they do. Unfortunately, disagreement over fundamental theoretical issues has led to stalemate, with entrenched camps of LLM optimists and pessimists often committed to very different views of how these systems work. Overcoming stalemate requires agreement on fundamental questions, and the goal of this paper is to address one such question, namely: is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up? This is a question about what kind of algorithm LLMs implement, and the answer carries serious implications for higher level questions about whether these systems have beliefs, intentions, concepts, knowledge, and understanding. I argue that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, and then I describe and defend a series of practical techniques for investigating these representations and developing explanations on their basis. The resulting account provides a groundwork for future theorizing about language models and their successors.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Steering Effectiveness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can the reliability of activation-based steering in LLMs be diagnosed using internal model signals such as entropy and KL divergence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that internal mechanistic signals (NBF and KL divergence) can predict steering effectiveness and introduces rotation-based steering as a stronger baseline for activation-based steering methods.
papers.conclusion: Internal mechanistic signals can predict steering effectiveness, and rotation-based steering provides a stronger baseline for activation-based steering methods, making steering a more measurable and predictable process.
papers.key_findings:
LLM judges (ChatGPT-4o-mini and Gemini-Flash-2.5) show substantial agreement in evaluating steering outputs after correcting for calibration bias.
Effective steering is characterized by structured entropy preservation (NBF) and coherent KL alignment across decoding steps.
Internal signals (NBF, KL, attention patterns) can predict steering quality with reasonable accuracy.
Rotation-based steering outperforms naive additive steering in terms of steering-coherence trade-off.
Attention patterns show a drop in confidence immediately after the intervention layer, correlating with coherence.
papers.limitation:
Limited conceptual coverage (only nine target concepts).
Focus on GEMMA model family, may not generalize to newer models.
Regression formulation requires further refinement.
Label noise from LLM-based judges and qualitative nature of tasks.
papers.abstract: Activation-based steering enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to exhibit targeted behaviors by intervening on intermediate activations without retraining. Despite its widespread use, the mechanistic factors that govern when steering succeeds or fails remain poorly understood, as prior work has relied primarily on black-box outputs or LLM-based judges. In this study, we investigate whether the reliability of steering can be diagnosed using internal model signals. We focus on two information-theoretic measures: the entropy-derived Normalized Branching Factor (NBF), and the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between steered activations and targeted concepts in the vocabulary space. We hypothesize that effective steering corresponds to structured entropy preservation and coherent KL alignment across decoding steps. Building on a reliability study demonstrating high inter-judge agreement between two architecturally distinct LLMs, we use LLM-generated annotations as ground truth and show that these mechanistic signals provide meaningful predictive power for identifying successful steering and estimating failure probability. We further introduce a stronger evaluation baseline for Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and Sparse Autoencoder-based steering, the two most widely adopted activation-steering methods.

papers.title: Unraveling Text Generation in LLMs: A Stochastic Differential Equation Approach
papers.research_question: How can Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) be used to model and interpret the text generation process of Large Language Models (LLMs), capturing both deterministic trends and stochastic variations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel mathematical framework based on Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) to model the text generation process in LLMs, capturing both deterministic trends (drift) and stochastic variations (diffusion) to enhance interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The SDE-based approach provides a dynamic and flexible method for modeling text generation in LLMs, effectively balancing consistency with creativity, though challenges remain with complex language structures.
papers.key_findings:
The SDE-based model effectively learns to balance coherence and variability in text generation.
The drift term captures deterministic trends and the general direction of text generation.
The diffusion term manages randomness and stochastic variations.
Trajectory analysis shows the model's predictions align well with actual text in simple contexts but deviate in more complex linguistic structures.
Analysis of word importance and attention weights reveals how key tokens influence the generation process.
papers.limitation: The model faces challenges in handling more complex language structures, indicating a need for further refinement of the drift and diffusion terms.
future_direction: Improving the drift and diffusion terms to better handle nuanced linguistic contexts.
Integrating the SDE-based interpretation method with other explainable AI techniques like attention visualization or feature attribution methods.
Extending the work to multi-modal language models that incorporate both text and visual information.
papers.abstract: This paper explores the application of Stochastic Differential Equations (SDE) to interpret the text generation process of Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT-4. Text generation in LLMs is modeled as a stochastic process where each step depends on previously generated content and model parameters, sampling the next word from a vocabulary distribution. We represent this generation process using SDE to capture both deterministic trends and stochastic perturbations. The drift term describes the deterministic trends in the generation process, while the diffusion term captures the stochastic variations. We fit these functions using neural networks and validate the model on real-world text corpora. Through numerical simulations and comprehensive analyses, including drift and diffusion analysis, stochastic process property evaluation, and phase space exploration, we provide deep insights into the dynamics of text generation. This approach not only enhances the understanding of the inner workings of LLMs but also offers a novel mathematical perspective on language generation, which is crucial for diagnosing, optimizing, and controlling the quality of generated text.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: I Predict Therefore I Am: Is Next Token Prediction Enough to Learn Human-Interpretable Concepts from Data?
papers.research_question: Is next-token prediction sufficient for large language models to learn human-interpretable concepts from data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes that LLM representations learned via next-token prediction are approximately a linear transformation of the log-posterior of latent human-interpretable concepts, providing a theoretical foundation for the linear representation hypothesis and motivating a principled evaluation method for sparse autoencoders.
papers.conclusion: Next-token prediction enables LLMs to learn human-interpretable concepts, and the linear identifiability result offers a unified perspective on the linear representation hypothesis and a principled approach for evaluating concept disentanglement methods like sparse autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
Under mild conditions, LLM representations are approximately a linear transformation of the log-posterior of latent concepts.
This linear property provides a unified explanation for empirical phenomena like concepts as directions and linear probing.
The linear property motivates a principled evaluation method for sparse autoencoders using linear probes.
Structured SAEs, which incorporate low-rank regularization, improve concept disentanglement compared to standard SAEs.
Empirical validation on simulation data and multiple LLM families (Pythia, Llama, DeepSeek) supports the theoretical results.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis relies on assumptions such as the diversity condition and approximate invertibility, which may not hold in all scenarios.
The evaluation of sparse autoencoders depends on the quality of linear probes, which may be noisy.
future_direction: Rethinking invertibility assumptions in causal representation learning.
Embedding causal reasoning in LLMs through linear unmixing.
papers.abstract: The remarkable achievements of large language models (LLMs) have led many to conclude that they exhibit a form of intelligence. This is as opposed to explanations of their capabilities based on their ability to perform relatively simple manipulations of vast volumes of data. To illuminate the distinction between these explanations, we introduce a novel generative model that generates tokens on the basis of human-interpretable concepts represented as latent discrete variables. Under mild conditions, even when the mapping from the latent space to the observed space is non-invertible, we establish an identifiability result, i.e., the representations learned by LLMs through next-token prediction can be approximately modeled as the logarithm of the posterior probabilities of these latent discrete concepts given input context, up to an invertible linear transformation. This theoretical finding not only provides evidence that LLMs capture underlying generative factors, but also provide a unified prospective for understanding of the linear representation hypothesis. Taking this a step further, our finding motivates a reliable evaluation of sparse autoencoders by treating the performance of supervised concept extractors as an upper bound. Pushing this idea even further, it inspires a structural variant that enforces dependence among latent concepts in addition to promoting sparsity. Empirically, we validate our theoretical results through evaluations on both simulation data and the Pythia, Llama, and DeepSeek model families, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our structured sparse autoencoder.

papers.title: NoiseGrad — Enhancing Explanations by Introducing Stochasticity to Model Weights
papers.research_question: Can introducing stochasticity in the weight parameter space enhance both local and global explanation methods for deep neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes NoiseGrad, a method that enhances local and global explanation methods by introducing stochasticity to model weights via sampling from a tempered Bayes posterior, and shows it outperforms SmoothGrad and its combination (FusionGrad) further improves performance.
papers.conclusion: Introducing stochasticity in the parameter space enhances XAI methods, with NoiseGrad improving both local and global explanations, facilitating practical and reliable XAI for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
NoiseGrad improves attribution quality (localization, faithfulness, robustness, sparseness) compared to baseline and SmoothGrad.
FusionGrad, combining NoiseGrad and SmoothGrad, yields the best performance across evaluation metrics.
NoiseGrad enhances global explanation methods like activation maximization, producing more vivid and human-interpretable feature visualizations.
A simple heuristic for setting the noise hyperparameter based on a 5% relative accuracy drop works well across architectures.
NoiseGrad is method-agnostic and computationally more expensive than SmoothGrad due to the larger number of parameters.
papers.limitation:
NoiseGrad is more computationally expensive than SmoothGrad because the number of parameters in a DNN is usually larger than the number of features in the input data.
Explanation evaluation is still an unsolved problem in XAI research and each evaluation technique comes with individual drawbacks.
future_direction: Investigate the performance of NoiseGrad and FusionGrad on other tasks such as time-series prediction or NLP.

Explore how NoiseGrad and FusionGrad explanations change when alternative ways of adding noise to the weights are employed, e.g., by adding different levels of noise to different layers or individual neurons.
papers.abstract: Many efforts have been made for revealing the decision-making process of black-box learning machines such as deep neural networks, resulting in useful local and global explanation methods.
